blocks.markdown:
Today's big question: how do rivers, mountains and climate shape life on Earth?

We will explore the physical world.
blocks.say: Welcome, explorer of Earth! Our big question: how do rivers, mountains and climates shape the places where plants, animals and people live? We will follow a river from source to sea, build mountains from a towel, and meet the biomes of the world. This is a game, not a test. Let's go!

blocks.alt: Rivers, mountains and climates shape our planet.
blocks.caption: Rivers, mountains and climates shape our planet.

terms.meaning: To do with the natural world, like rivers and mountains.

blocks.text: Stop 1: The journey of a river

blocks.markdown:
A river begins at its **source** and ends at its **mouth**, where it meets the sea.

A smaller river that joins a bigger one is called a **tributary**.
blocks.say: Every river has a journey from start to finish. It begins at a place called the source, often high in the hills or mountains, where rain falls or snow and ice melt. Smaller streams join to make a bigger river. A smaller river that joins a bigger one is called a tributary. Finally, the river reaches the sea, and the place where it meets the sea is called the mouth. Along its journey, a river carves valleys and carries soil and stones downstream.

blocks.title: A river from source to mouth

blocks.markdown:
Rivers give water for **crops**, drinking and travel.

Many cities were built beside rivers.
blocks.say: People have always settled near rivers. Rivers give us water to drink and to grow crops. They are used for travel and for carrying goods. Rich soil, left behind when rivers flood, helps crops grow. The Indus, the Nile and the Thames all had cities beside them. But rivers can flood and be polluted too, so we must take care of them.

blocks.markdown:
The Earth's surface is made of huge **tectonic plates** that move very slowly.

When plates push together, the land folds upwards into **fold mountains**.
blocks.say: The Earth's surface is not one piece. It is broken into huge slabs called tectonic plates, which move very slowly, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Sometimes two plates push against each other. The land between them crumples and folds upwards, like a rug pushed from both ends. This makes fold mountains. The Himalaya and the Karakoram in the north of Pakistan formed this way, over millions of years.

scenes.caption: Two plates, side by side.
scenes.say: Here are two plates of land, side by side.

scenes.caption: The plates push together.
scenes.say: They move towards each other, very slowly, and push together.

scenes.caption: The land folds into mountains.
scenes.say: The land between them has nowhere to go but up. Over millions of years, it folds into mountains.

blocks.title: Make fold mountains
materials: A towel or a sheet of paper
instructions: Lay the towel flat on the table. This is the Earth's surface.
Put a hand on each end and slowly push your hands together.
Watch what happens in the middle. The towel folds up into ridges!
What would happen if you pushed for a million years?

question.prompt: What happens when two plates push together?
question.explanation: The land crumples and folds into mountains.

blocks.markdown:
The higher the **altitude**, the colder it gets.

The peaks of high mountains are snowy all year.
blocks.say: Have you noticed that mountain tops are cold? The higher up we go, the colder the air becomes, about six degrees cooler for every thousand metres. The height of land above the sea is called altitude. That is why the tops of high mountains like K2 are covered in snow and ice all year, even in a hot country. And high up, the air is thin, so climbers need extra oxygen.

blocks.markdown:
**Climate** is the usual weather of a place over many years.

The **equator** is the imaginary line round the middle of the Earth. Places near it are hot.
blocks.say: Weather changes from day to day, but climate is the usual weather of a place over many years. The Earth has different climate zones. Near the middle of the Earth, around a line called the equator, the Sun's rays shine most strongly, so it is hot all year. This is the tropical zone. Some places are dry, with very little rain: these are deserts. Further north and south the climate is temperate, with mild weather and four seasons. And near the North and South Poles it is polar: bitterly cold.

scenes.caption: Tropical: hot all year.
scenes.say: In the tropical zone near the equator, it is hot and often wet all year. A typical day is thirty degrees.

scenes.caption: Desert: very hot and dry.
scenes.say: In the desert zone, the days are very hot and it hardly ever rains. It can reach forty degrees.

scenes.caption: Temperate: mild.
scenes.say: In the temperate zone, like the UK, the weather is mild. A typical day is twelve degrees, with four seasons.

scenes.caption: Polar: freezing cold.
scenes.say: In the polar zone, it is freezing. A typical day can be twenty degrees below zero.

question.prompt: Which climate zone is hot all year, near the equator?
question.hint: The Sun shines most strongly there.
question.explanation: The tropical zone is hot all year.

blocks.markdown: Pakistan has several climates. The plains are hot, the mountains are cold.
blocks.say: Pakistan has a mix. Much of it is hot and dry, especially the south and the deserts. In the north, high in the mountains, it is cold, even polar on the highest peaks. The lower, greener north and the plains of Punjab have four seasons. So a small country can hold several climates, because altitude changes the weather as well as the distance from the equator.

blocks.markdown:
A **biome** is a huge area with a similar climate, plants and animals.

Living things are **adapted** to the biome they live in.
blocks.say: A biome is a huge area with a similar climate, and with plants and animals that are suited to it. In a desert, plants like cacti store water, and camels can go many days without a drink. In a rainforest it is warm and wet, so thousands of different plants and animals live there. Grasslands have wide plains with grass and animals that graze. Forests are full of trees. And the tundra is frozen and treeless. Each living thing is adapted to its biome.

scenes.caption: Desert.
scenes.say: In the desert it is hot and dry. A cactus stores water, and a camel can go many days without a drink.

scenes.caption: Rainforest.
scenes.say: In the rainforest it is warm and wet, with tall trees and colourful birds.

scenes.caption: Grassland.
scenes.say: On the grassland, lions and zebras roam across the wide plain.

scenes.caption: Tundra.
scenes.say: In the cold tundra, polar bears have thick fur and a layer of fat to keep warm.

question.prompt: Which animal is adapted to the desert?
question.hint: It can go days without water.
question.explanation: A camel stores energy and can live with little water.

blocks.markdown:
An **adaptation** helps a living thing survive in its home.

Protecting biomes protects the animals that live in them.
blocks.say: Adaptation means a body part or behaviour that helps a living thing survive in its home. A camel has wide feet to walk on sand and a hump that stores fat. A polar bear has thick fur and a layer of fat. A parrot has a strong beak to crack nuts and bright feathers. If a living thing moved to the wrong biome, it might not survive. That is why protecting biomes protects the animals living in them.

blocks.alt: Each animal is adapted to its biome.
blocks.caption: Each animal is adapted to its biome.

blocks.prompt: Why couldn't a polar bear live in the desert?
blocks.answer_markdown: It has thick fur and fat to stay warm in the cold. In the hot desert, it would overheat and could not find the food it needs.
